items.title: Fine for animal bedding manufacturer after worker loses fingers in machinery
items.summary: Norfolk-based company that specialises in horse and pet bedding fined after incident Worker had two fingers severed while trying to unblock machinery HSE investigation found machinery was not properly guarded A company that specialises in bedding for horses and pets has been fined after one of its workers severed fingers in machinery. The man had […]
items.body:
- Norfolk-based company that specialises in horse and pet bedding fined after incident
- Worker had two fingers severed while trying to unblock machinery
- HSE investigation found machinery was not properly guarded
A company that specialises in bedding for horses and pets has been fined after one of its workers severed fingers in machinery.
The man had been working for Bed Down LLP at its site in Metfield, Norfolk when the incident happened on 1 May 2024. The production operative had been attempting to remove a piece of wood that had become lodged in a bespoke large planer machine. As he did so, he partially severed the middle and ring fingers on his left hand.
The bespoke planer machine is used by the company to create wood shavings from timber logs. There had been several blockages throughout the day, and the man had opened the steel access door to remove another piece of wood that had become lodged.
The incident resulted in injuries which have profoundly impacted the victim’s life. He underwent surgery and months of physiotherapy. More than two years later, he continues to experience pain, reduced dexterity, flashbacks, and the ongoing impact of his injuries on both his personal and working life.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the machine’s access doors were not fitted with interlocking guards. As a result, dangerous moving parts continued to operate when the doors were opened, allowing workers access to the cutter head blades while the machine remained in motion. Following the incident, interlock switches were installed to ensure that the machine automatically stopped whenever an access door was opened, so preventing access to dangerous moving parts.
The law requires employers to take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery or to stop their movement before any part of a person’s body can enter a danger zone. Such measures include fixed guards and, where these are not reasonably practicable, other suitable guards or protective devices. Machinery hazards should be identified through suitable and sufficient risk assessments, with appropriate control measures implemented to eliminate or reduce the risk of injury.
Bed Down LLP, of Cherry Tree Farm, The Common, Metfield, Norfolk, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998. The company was fined £20,000 and ordered to pay costs of £8,000 at Great Yarmouth Magistrate Court on 20 November 2026.
HSE Inspector Adepeju Sogadgi said:
“This worker suffered wholly preventable injuries while attempting to clear a blockage on machinery while cutters were exposed, accessible and fully operational.
“The dangers associated with moving machinery are well known, which is why such basic failures are deeply disheartening. Employers must always ensure effective measures are in place to prevent workers accessing dangerous parts.
“If suitable interlocking arrangements and a safe system of work been in place, this incident could easily have been prevented.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Chloe Ward, supported by paralegal Thomas Smith.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- Relevant guidance can be found at: PUWER
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found here.

items.title: HTY & Anor, R (on the application of) v Competition and Markets Authority (Anonymity)
items.body:
Royal Courts of Justice,
Strand, London, WC2A 2LL
Before:
The Hon. Mrs Justice Steyn DBE
Between:
| THE KING on the application of (1) HTY (2) HTN | Claimants | 
| - and - |  | 
| COMPETITION AND MARKETS AUTHORITY | Defendant | 
Adam Wolanski KC and Felicity McMahon (instructed by Winston Taylor) for the Claimants
Marie Demetriou KC and Richard Howell (instructed by Competition and Markets Authority) for the Defendant
Hearing date: 24 November 2026
JUDGMENT
MRS JUSTICE STEYN:
Introduction
By this claim for judicial review, the claimants seek to challenge an information notice dated 12 December 2025 (‘the Notice’) issued by the Competition and Markets Authority (‘the CMA’), in exercise of statutory powers conferred by Parliament for the protection of consumers. The CMA had not, when issuing the Notice, and has not yet, decided whether to open an investigation. The Notice stated: "The CMA has not formed a view on whether there may be infringements of UK consumer law and is approaching its enquiries with an open mind."
The claim has been listed together with the claim brought by Ryanair DAC and others against the CMA (AC-2026-LON-003660) for a three-day rolled-up hearing beginning today.
When filing the claim on 10 March 2026, the claimants also made an application for anonymity, seeking urgent consideration. That application was granted by Lang J on 11 March 2026. By her order, she granted the claimants anonymity, directing that their names are to be withheld and must not be disclosed in any proceedings in public; she made a reporting restriction in respect of their identities and an order pursuant to CPR 5.4C, which has the effect that no non-party may obtain a copy of any unredacted statement of case without the court's permission.
The application was determined before the CMA had an opportunity to make written submissions in response to it, although their letter of 25 February 2026 which put forward many of the arguments pursued today was exhibited to the witness statement of Mr Crown which was before the court. Lang J's reasons for granting anonymity were as follows:
"The claimants have a reasonable expectation of confidentiality at this stage and would be likely to suffer significant reputational damage if they were publicly identified. In the circumstances, a departure from the general principle of open justice is justified."
This is my judgment on the CMA's application to discharge the anonymity order. That application has been supported by the Press Association, which has filed written submissions, and it is opposed by the claimants. As Mr Wolanski KC accepted, on behalf of the claimants, it is for the court to consider anonymity afresh.
The legal principles
The starting point is the principle of open justice, which is "one of the most precious in our law" and "of cardinal importance": R (C) v Secretary of State for Justice [2016] 1WLR 444, Baroness Hale, [1]; JIH v News Group Newspapers Limited [2011] 1WLR 1646, Lord Neuberger, [19]. The ordinary position is that hearings take place in public and the parties are named.Open justice entails that "the public has a right to know not only what is going on in our courts, but also who the principal actors are": R (C) v Secretary of State for Justice, [36] and [18]. Identification of the parties is itself an important aspect of open justice.Lord Rodger's judgment in In re Guardian News and Media Limited [2010] 2 AC 697, in which he famously asked, "What's in a name? ‘A lot’, the press would answer", "vividly illustrates the importance of being able to identify and put a name to parties to litigation which is potentially of interest to the public":JIH, [36]. Names provide context.They enable the press to report proceedings in a way that is concrete and intelligible, rather than abstract or disembodied.Such reports are of more interest to their readers and so more likely to be published and to contribute to public debate: Guardian News, [63]-[64]; R (C) v Secretary of State for Justice, [18]-[19]; JIH, [35]-[36].
As Popplewell LJ observed in R (Wright) v Medway Magistrates' Court [2026] EWHC 1842 at [52(2)], when addressing the general rule that the administration of justice must be done in public and the public has a right to know who the principal actors are:
"This reflects two strong public interests enshrined in rights of freedom of expression in article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). One is journalistic freedom of expression, which applies to all media reporting to which questions of the public interest are given particular prominence by s.12(4) Human Rights Act 1998. This reflects the role of a free press in a democratic society to act as a ‘watchdog’ and ‘bloodhound’ (see e.g. ZXC at [59]-[62]). The second is specific to court proceedings and is the public interest in open justice by reason of the value of public scrutiny as a guarantor of the quality of justice so as to promote public confidence in the administration of justice (see Khuja at [13] and ZXC at [77])."
The open justice principle is not absolute: JIH, [20]. The court may anonymise the identity of a party, restrict access to court documents and impose corresponding reporting restrictions. But such derogations "can only be justified if truly exceptional and strictly necessary, and the justification must be established by ‘clear and cogent evidence’":Wright v Medway Magistrates, [3], citing Rai and Marandi; Practice Guidance (Interim Non-Disclosure Orders) [2012] 1 WLR 1003. Popplewell LJ explained at [52(3)] of Wright v Medway Magistrates:
"It is not that rights under article 8 and article 10 of ECHR have any intrinsic priority over the other, but rather that the weight to be accorded to the article 10 rights involved in the principle of open justice is very considerable."
The fundamental principles of open justice remain clearly and succinctly set out in the Master of the Rolls’ Practice Guidance: see Secake v Shared Services Connected Ltd [2026] EWHC 1022 (KB), Saini J, [15]. Notably there is no general exception to open justice where privacy or confidentiality is in issue; and the burden of establishing any derogation from the general principle lies on the person seeking it: Practice Guidance, [12]-[13]. As Saini J observed in Secake at [16]:
"In accordance with the requirement to establish the necessity for any derogation from open justice with clear and cogent evidence, the court will scrutinise with care any application that the court should withhold the name of a party or other details about the claim (from the public). Mere assertion that a party may suffer some harm is unlikely to discharge the burden to justify the order."
The rival submissions
The claimants resist the application to discharge the anonymity order. They submit that the court must weigh the contribution that identifying them would make to open justice, and the harm it would cause, together with any engaged Convention Rights. They contend that naming them would contribute little, if anything, given the nature of the issues before the court.
They submit that they retain a reasonable expectation of confidentiality in the fact and subject matter of the CMA's preliminary enquiries. Their case is that the Notice contains information not in the public domain and was communicated in circumstances expressly imposing confidentiality. They refer to the terms of the Notice, which emphasised forcefully the confidentiality of the CMA's enquiries. The Notice stated that they should not disclose the Notice or its contents, or the fact of the CMA's enquiries without prior agreement of the CMA, other than to their legal or economic advisers, and warned that disclosure of “specified information” may constitute a criminal offence under section 245(3) of the Enforcement Act 2002. The notice was marked "Official - Sensitive". The claimants criticise the stance taken by the CMA in relation to the confidentiality of the Notice, contending that they have performed a volte-face.
The claimants characterise the statutory scheme as providing a calibrated threshold for publicity. Reasonable grounds for suspecting an infringement must exist before a formal investigation is opened, at which point the CMA may publish a notice identifying those under investigation pursuant to s.180 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024. They draw an analogy with the protection of individuals against identification during pre-charge criminal investigations considered in ZXC v Bloomberg [2022] AC 1158, submitting that direct enforcement proceedings are criminal for article 6 purposes, because of the potentially substantial penal financial sanctions. They rely on article 8 of the ECHR, contending that as legal persons their communications are afforded protection by that provision. However, Mr Wolanski submits that, whether or not article 8 rights are engaged, the claimants’ right to confidentiality and their reasonable expectation of privacy are engaged and fall to be considered pursuant to CPR 39.2(4).
In the witness statement accompanying their anonymity application, Mr Crown stated that the Notice would be "likely to be construed by the public as founded upon a belief that the HTY Claimants have in fact engaged in consumer law infringements". He asserted that press coverage "... framed in terms of suspected wrongdoing and consumer harm" would cause "immediate and irreversible harm to the HTY Claimants' interests". The claimants submit that requiring them to surrender confidentiality in order to challenge the Notice would inhibit access to justice and deter similar challenges. They contend there's been no material change since the anonymity order was made, enquiries remain preliminary, and the reasons Lang J gave for granting anonymity continue to apply.
The CMA, supported by the Press Association who have filed written submissions, acknowledges that there has been no material change of circumstances. Their case is that anonymity was never justified. The CMA did not have an opportunity to make written submissions before the order was made, albeit their letter was before the court. And the Press Association had no opportunity to make representations prior to the grant of anonymity as the application for anonymity was not served on the media. The Press Association obtained a copy following my order of 18 November 2026.
The CMA contends that, applying the principles to which I have referred, anonymity is not necessary to protect the claimants' interests or to secure the proper administration of justice.
The CMA acknowledges that its enquiries have been conducted confidentially and that the wording in the Notice was liable to convey a misleading impression as to the legal restrictions on disclosure. The template on which the Notice was based has since been amended. An error on the part of the CMA cannot waive the public's right to open justice.
The CMA contends that article 8 does not protect corporate reputation. However, in her oral submissions, Ms Demetriou KC emphasised that their case is that the outcome is clear, the anonymity order should be discharged, whether or not article 8 is engaged.
The CMA is willing to proceed on the assumption for the purposes of consideration of this application that a financial penalty could engage the autonomous criminal limb of article 6 of the ECHR, but contends it remains significant that these are enquiries concerning civil enforcement unlike in ZXC. In any event, ZXC concerned media publication not open justice.
The CMA characterises the evidence of harm as generalised and speculative. The Press Association develops that submission, noting that the requirement that reports of legal proceedings should be fair and accurate dictates that any publications regarding the case will state that no formal investigation has been launched, that the claimants wish to co-operate with the CMA, and that it is alleged that the CMA has acted unlawfully by issuing the Notice.
Decision
Applying the principles I have identified, the court must begin by according very substantial weight to open justice and article 10. I accept that even if the claimants were to remain anonymised, the proceedings and judgment would remain public and reportable, and from the court's perspective the identity of the claimants is not of any particular significance in determining the claims. But that does not detract from the public's right to know who the principal actors are in this litigation and to understand the context in which the CMA has sought to exercise its powers. If the claimants remain anonymised that would be likely to reduce reporting of their claim and so lessen public discussion of and engagement with the CMA's use of its powers to protect consumer rights.
I agree that whether or not article 8 is engaged is not determinative: the outcome is the same in either case. Nonetheless it is of some significance to consider whether or not there are Convention rights engaged on both sides of the balance or only on one side.
Would setting aside the anonymity order engage article 8 rights? The harm that the claimants have focused on is harm to reputation. While I accept that legal persons have some rights under article 8 (for example, business premises are covered by the notion of home, and their communications are covered by the notion of correspondence: Ships Waste Oil Collector BV v Netherlands (2799/16) (2026) 83 EHRR 1), it does not follow that they have an article 8 right to reputation. The right to protection of reputation (which is not expressly mentioned in article 8) is a right which is protected by article 8 "as part of the right to respect for private life":ZXC, [118] and [120]. Moreover, "it is not enough in order for article 8 to be engaged that the individual will suffer damage to reputation as a result of publication. The injury to reputation must be sufficiently serious to amount to an interference with rights to a private life":Wright v Medway Magistrates, [52(6)]; ZXC, [121].
The claimants are corporate entities, which do not have private lives, so any risk of harm to their reputations does not engage article 8. I agree with the CMA that Dana Astra v Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs [2025] EWHC 289 (Admin), Saini J, [63], and Euromoney Institutional Investor v Aviation News Ltd [2013] EWHC 1505 (QB), Tugendhat J, [20], provide some support for the conclusion that article 8 does not protect a right to corporate reputation.
The claimants rely on the right to respect for correspondence which covers the communications of legal persons. But how would discharging any anonymity order interfere with that right? They have chosen to bring a claim. In accordance with paragraph 2.4 of Practice Direction 16, the full names of each of the HTY claimants were stated in the claim form. Neither that requirement nor the ordinary position that the names of parties are publicised on the cause list and non-parties may access the statements of case constitutes an interference with their correspondence such as to engage article 8. It seems to me that the position is no different here where the CMA seeks to set aside an anonymity order with the effect that those ordinary rules would apply.
For these reasons, I am not persuaded that any article 8 rights that the claimants may have would be engaged in a decision to set aside the anonymity order, such that they should be weighed in the balance against the article 10 rights and the open justice principle that are engaged.
Nonetheless, as I have said, I recognise that the claimants do have interests to be weighed in the balance. At present, the fact and content of CMA's enquiries of them are not in the public domain and so remain confidential. The Notice asserted that confidentiality in strong terms. But the fact that the Notice was confidential is wholly insufficient, in my view, to justify an exception to open justice. There is no general exception to open justice for private or confidential information. Parties to litigation frequently have to accept that a price of litigating is that information will be aired in public which otherwise would not enter the public domain. As Saini J observed in Secake at [18]:
"There are many examples of claimants in other areas who would wish to avoid the publicity of legal proceedings which are likely to cause them additional stress and hurt over and above the civil wrong to which they have been subject."
Mr Wolanski emphasised that the statutory scheme creates a trigger point when publication is justified. It seems to me the effect of the argument based on the stage of the CMA's enquiries, if accepted, would be to create a class of claims in which claimants would ordinarily be entitled to anonymity because they are challenging a notice of the kind in issue in this case. There is no sound basis nor compelling justification for adopting such an approach, which would amount to a significant inroad into open justice: see XXX v Camden Borough Council [2020] 4 WLR 165, [18] and [25].
In my judgment, ZXC does not assist the claimants. First, as I have indicated, I am not persuaded that they have an article 8 right to reputation. But if that is wrong, as Popplewell LJ observed in Wright v Medway Magistrates at [52(6)]:
"The status of a businessman in a high profile role in a public company can diminish the weight to be attached to article 8 rights because such a person has a lesser expectation of privacy in relation to the affairs of the company: ZXC at [140]."
If the claimants have rights to reputation that are protected by article 8, logically this point must apply all the more forcefully to such a company itself, so further diminishing the weight to be attached to such rights. And, in my view, it also lessens the weight to be attached to their right to confidentiality and reasonable expectation of privacy outside of any article 8 rights.
Secondly, ZXC concerned media reporting not open justice. As Popplewell LJ observed in Wright v Medway Justices at [58], ZXC is not determinative of whether Article 8 rights are engaged, and "the case has nothing to say about that balancing exercise in the context of the open justice principle, which raises different considerations from mere journalistic freedom of expression, which was the only article 10 consideration which arose in that case".
Thirdly, the CMA’s enquiries concern whether it should exercise its civil enforcement functions. Assuming (as I have been invited to do) that the imposition of a penalty would involve the determination of a criminal charge within the autonomous meaning of article 6, nonetheless, the analogy drawn with ZXC which concerned a criminal investigation in the core sense of that term is somewhat stretched. This is a minor point but I agree with the CMA that it further lessens the weight to be given to the claimants' rights to reputation and to confidentiality.
Assessment of the risk of harm and the likely extent of harm if the claimants are identified is a question of fact rather than of law. In my judgment, the evidence on behalf of the claimants is speculative and overstates the risk. While, realistically, there may well be members of the public who assume the worst, the extent to which that is likely to be the case is bound to be influenced by the information provided to the public. This judgment makes clear that the CMA has not even decided to open an investigation, so it has not at this stage even made a determination that there is a reasonable suspicion the claimants have infringed consumer law. Media organisations will be conscious that to avail themselves of the privilege that applies in respect of reports of court proceedings, their reports would have to be fair and accurate and reflect such points. Moreover, if they felt it necessary to do so, the claimants themselves have a voice and would be well placed to counter unfair reporting, mitigating any impact.
Accordingly, I conclude that maintaining the anonymity of the claimants is not necessary to secure the proper administration of justice or to protect the interests of any person. The test in CPR 39.2(4) is not met and so I will set aside the anonymity order.
