items.body:
Judgment approved by the Court for handing down Oziel v Sainsbury's
Rolls Building
Fetter Lane, London, EC4A 1NL
Before :
HER HONOUR JUDGE JOFFE
Between :
MISS DEBORAH OZIEL
Appellant
- and –
SAINSBURY’S SUPERMARKETS LIMITED
Respondent
Miss Oziel the Appellant appeared in person
Mr T Welch (instructed by TLT Solicitors) for the Respondent
Hearing date: 24 September 2026
JUDGMENT
SUMMARY
Sex discrimination, whistleblowing
The principal ground of appeal was whether the Tribunal erred in failing to identify and determine claims of discriminatory constructive dismissal and automatically unfair dismissal for having made public interest disclosures (section 103A ERA 1996). Those legal labels had not been identified for the claims either in the claimant's claim form or in the list of issues agreed at a case management preliminary hearing. Both documents listed the acts of discrimination and the public interest disclosure detriments as breaches of the implied term of trust and confidence or conduct which contributed to a breach of the implied term.
The claimant had resigned after a series of events which included incidents of aggressive treatment by a colleague which the Tribunal found to be direct sex discrimination and various failures by the respondent in its handling of the complaints made by the claimant and her colleague, which the Tribunal found were detriments because the claimant had made a public interest disclosure. The Tribunal found that these and other matters amounted to a breach of the implied term of trust and confidence and that the claimant had been constructively dismissed and that dismissal was unfair, pursuant to section 98 ERA1996.
In determining remedy, the Tribunal therefore capped the claimant's compensation for financial losses under section 124 (1ZA) ERA 1996.
The claimant appealed a number of aspects of the remedy decision.
Held, allowing the liability appeal and a number of grounds of appeal in respect of remedy:
The Tribunal should have identified and decided the discriminatory constructive dismissal and section 103A ERA 1996 claims. Applying the principles derived from the authorities distilled in Moustache v Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust [2025] EWCA Civ 185, those claims were present on an objective reading of the claim form and had not been abandoned. Alternatively, they should have been identified by the Tribunal as part of its duty of fairness;
Applying Al Jumard v Clywd Leisure Ltd [2008] IRLR 345, the Tribunal should have analysed the injury to feelings arising from the sex discrimination claims and that caused by the public interest disclosure detriments separately, since the claims arose from different acts;
Having found that an Acas uplift was appropriate, the Tribunal should have considered whether and to what extent to apply the uplift to the injury to feelings award;
The Tribunal had erred in basing its award for injury to feelings in part on a finding that the claimant had a history of depression and anxiety in circumstances where that finding was unsupported by evidence;
The Tribunal had failed to provide adequate reasons for applying a midpoint in its calculation of interest for injury to feelings and for not grossing up the award.
HER HONOUR JUDGE JOFFE:
Introduction
This is an appeal from a judgment of EJ Bartlett sitting with members, Mr Miller and Mrs Hancock, sent to the parties on 14 August 2024.
The parties are referred to as the claimant and respondent as they were before the Employment Tribunal.
The judgment followed a full merits hearing heard at Watford over five days between 3 and 7 June 2024. On 7 June 2024, the Tribunal gave an oral judgment on liability with reasons and then proceeded to consider remedy. There is a transcript of day five of the proceedings which has been provided on this appeal. The claimant represented herself at the full merits hearing.
The claimant’s claims were in the main upheld. There was an ordinary constructive unfair dismissal claim pursuant to section 98 Employment Rights Act 1996, claims of public interest disclosure detriment under section 47B ERA 1996, and direct sex discrimination claims under section 13 Equality Act 2010. A harassment claim on the same facts as the direct discrimination claims was dismissed because the claims had succeeded as direct discrimination. This appeal centres on the question of whether there were other claims arising from the claimant’s constructive dismissal which it was an error of law for the Tribunal to fail to identify; there are separate challenges to the Tribunal’s remedy findings.
Background
I take the following condensed account from the Tribunal’s detailed reasons.
The claimant made a number of complaints which she said collectively amounted to a breach of the implied tern of trust and confidence. A subset of these were claims of sex discrimination or harassment related to sex. A subset were claims of public interest disclosure detriment.
The claimant had worked at a small Sainsbury’s store in East Finchley from 15 June 2016. Sometimes there would only be one or two staff on site. The claimant was a ‘CTM’, which is a management position somewhere between supervisor and store manager. There were other CTMs as well as colleagues in a more junior position described as ‘responsible colleagues’. That included a Mr Henderson. The matters about which the claimant complained started some eighteen months before the claimant left her employment but the complaints were largely about events which occurred in the last few months.
The claimant alleged that Mr Henderson behaved aggressively towards her and other colleagues and customers and the Tribunal made findings that there had been incidents on several dates the claimant gave evidence about when Mr Henderson had behaved aggressively to the claimant.
On 23 September 2021, Mr Henderson had two consecutive outbursts against the claimant during the second of which he called her a ‘fucking bitch’.
The 23 September 2021 incident was investigated by the respondent in a way the Tribunal considered to have been not unreasonable.
In November / December 2021 the claimant was subject to an investigation in respect of a complaint made by a different colleague about her. The Tribunal found that the investigation was handled poorly; the claimant was not notified of the allegations prior to the investigation meeting or given advance warning of the meeting. She was not notified of an outcome and there were delays in the process.
On 25 January 2023, there was an incident where the claimant was seriously assaulted by two female shoplifters. The claimant was extremely distressed by the incident and the Tribunal found that she was offered no support by the respondent.
On 2 February 2023, Mr Henderson was abusive to a female colleague and a customer and told another colleague that he intended to buy an imitation gun to bring to the store to threaten the claimant with.
On 7 February 2023, Mr Henderson swore several times at the claimant in a confined space whilst blocking the only door.
The store manager to whom the claimant reported the incident laughed when the claimant mentioned the threat about the imitation gun and told the claimant that she took things too seriously and became over emotional.
The claimant that day sent the email containing what the Tribunal found to be her protected disclosure, which the Tribunal said included:
Allegations about Mr Henderson’s aggression to herself and others;
The allegation about the imitation gun.
The Tribunal noted, of the investigation that followed, that there was no investigation at all of the imitation gun issue, that the investigation was generally inadequate, and that it was hard to understand how the investigating manager reached the conclusion that ‘there was a breakdown in communication and that the situation was not handled correctly or appropriately by anyone involved’.
The Tribunal found that the investigation of the claimant’s complaint was in contrast with that of the complaint made by Mr Henderson, which latter investigation arrived at conclusions which were critical of the claimant. Mr Henderson’s complaint was treated as a grievance and the claimant’s was not.
On 8 March 2023, the claimant was told by a manager, Mr Curry, that she needed training in conflict management, that management had bullied Mr Henderson, and that the claimant had demonstrated poor management in dealing with Mr Henderson. The claimant was told she would have to enter into mediation with Mr Henderson and that refusal to do so was a refusal of a reasonable management request which could lead to further action against her.
On 13 March 2023, the claimant’s bodycam footage of her encounter with Mr Henderson on 7 February 2023 was deleted in circumstances where the Tribunal found it should have been saved, given the claimant’s complaints and the respondent’s own policy.
On 25 March 2023, the claimant sent the respondent a grievance. She resigned on 29 March 2023, not having received a response to her grievance at that point.
The grievance was investigated by Mr Curry. The Tribunal found his investigation to be ‘biased against the claimant and fundamentally flawed’. It found that he failed to investigate the imitation gun remark and instead the claimant was unfairly blamed for the situation with Mr Henderson and subject to unfair criticisms.
The claim form and list of issues
The claim form and list of issues are important to an understanding of the issues in this appeal.
At section 8 of the claim form, the claimant ticked the boxes for unfair dismissal and for discrimination on grounds of race, disability and sex. The attached particulars included a heading for constructive unfair dismissal, which set out complaints which included the incidents of aggression with Mr Henderson and the use of the word ‘bitch’. The claimant also said: ‘I see clear detriments being suffered as I reported breach of legal obligation in protecting myself, staff and customers from harm. There is an implied duty to provide a safe place of work and to prevent harm or injury to others.’
The particulars set out in respect of sex discrimination and public interest disclosure detriments were:
‘3.Sex Discrimination
The fact that Matthew said to me in 2 separate occasions “fuck you fucking bitch” & “shut the fuck up you stupid bitch” amounted to an act of direct sex discrimination. He would not have called a male supervisor the same way.
4.Whistle blow
Further, I have asserted that there has been a whistle blow. I have given information to the company that has tended to show that there has been or is likely to be a health and safety risk and or an unsafe place of work. In addition, I highlighted a likely criminal offence regarding Matthew who threatened to harm me and or bring into work an imitation firearm. That information above was a qualifying disclosure and it then became protected when I disclosed it to managers including HR. As a direct result I suffered detriments’
The Tribunal at the full merits hearing had a list of issues agreed at a case management preliminary hearing at which both parties were legally represented which was, so far as relevant, as follows:
‘Constructive Unfair dismissal
The conduct relied upon by the Claimant to establish a fundamental breach of
contract is:
No/inadequate action being taken in relation to or against Matthew Henderson, despite his incidents of aggression against the Claimant, her colleagues, and customers.
The lack of training/guidance provided in relation to dealing with staff
with disabilities.
The handling and conclusion of an allegation made in November 2021 against the Claimant (by Lukas Durilla).
The Claimant was subjected to two investigations that were not concluded (the first started on 17 December 2021 and the second, where new allegations were added, was scheduled for the 09 February 2022).
The process was unnecessarily delayed.
There was no/insufficient evidence to warrant the Claimant being formally investigated.
The Claimant was encouraged by the store manager, Nick Galvin, not to take formal action/complain about Matthew Henderson.
The handling of an incident with Matthew Henderson on 07 February 2023 where he was aggressive/inappropriate toward the Claimant:
The Claimant was blamed for the incident.
The Claimant was threatened with disciplinary proceedings if she did not attend mediation with Matthew Henderson.
The lack of support offered when the Claimant was involved in an incident with shoplifters on 25 January 2023.
Being discriminated against (see below).
Being subjected to detriments for making protected disclosures (see below) and the conduct set out in paragraph 29 below.
Did the above conduct occur as alleged by the Claimant? If so, did any of the conduct, or taken cumulatively, amount to a fundamental breach of contract? (the last straw in the chain of events being The Claimant’s bodycam footage of Matthew Henderson being moved/deleted from the internal portal on 13 March 2023.
…
Direct Sex Discrimination
Did the following less favourable treatment occur as alleged by the Claimant?
On 23 September 2021, Matthew Henderson shouted at the Claimant stating, “fuck you fucking bitch.”
On 07 February 2023, Matthew Henderson was shouting and being aggressive toward the Claimant and stating – “shut the fuck up you stupid bitch.”
…
Whistleblowing
Did the Claimant make a qualifying disclosure? The Claimant relies on:
07 February 2023 – Her email to Idrani Chowdhury, Yash Redman and “Ask HR” – reporting aggressive and threatening behaviour of Matthew Henderson toward staff and customers and that she and colleagues feared for their safety.
…
Did the Claimant suffer the following detriments on the grounds that she made a
protected disclosure? The Claimant alleges that:
The complaints about Matthew Henderson not being properly addressed or investigated.
There being no action taken against Matthew Henderson.
The Claimant being told by Nick Galvin not to complain about Matthew Henderson (07 February 2023).
The Claimant (on 08 March 2023) being told by Idrani Chowdhury:
That the Claimant needed training in conflict management.
That the Respondent felt like the situation with Matthew Henderson was dealt with incorrectly.
That the Respondent felt like management had bullied Matthew Henderson.
The Claimant being told she had to have a meeting/mediation with Matthew Henderson.
The Claimant being told that if she did not meet with Matthew Henderson, this was refusing a reasonable management request (and if she was ready to pay the consequences).
The Claimant’s bodycam footage of Matthew Henderson being moved/deleted from the internal portal (13 March 2023).’
[Emphasis added]
The Tribunal would have known that the claimant had representation by a solicitor at the case management hearing; otherwise she appeared to be representing herself. The respondent wished to rely for the purposes of the appeal on a costs schedule which was subsequently prepared by the claimant, which shows that she had some advice from a solicitor in preparing her particulars of claim. No representative was on the record for her or named in the ET1.
The Tribunal’s findings
The reasons set out the list of issues and note that ‘we have not followed the list of issues slavishly because some if it is incorrect, repetitive and vague’. The Tribunal did not itemise in what respects it had departed from the list but that is ultimately apparent from the findings it made.
The Tribunal found the two allegations of direct sex discrimination were made out.
It also found that all of the detriments pleaded were caused by the protected disclosure, apart from the claimant being told by Mr Galvin, store manager, not to complain about Mr Henderson on 7 February 2023, as that happened before the protected disclosure.
At paragraph 87 the Tribunal said:
‘We consider that the allegations are typical whistleblowing detriments and the sort of detriment that the Whistleblowing legislation was put in place to address. By this we mean that the claimant was seen as an annoyance for raising these allegations, it was thought that she should have dealt with the situation herself, she was blamed for the situation and raising these allegations was something that she should not have done. People involved in the allegations such as MH and NG disparaged the claimant and their disparagement was taken at face value. Again it is typical in whistleblowing situations that those directly or indirectly criticised in whistle blowing situations seek to blame the whistleblower. This is exactly what happened here and it was accepted without question. This led to the detriments which the claimant has identified.’
As for the constructive dismissal claim, the Tribunal found that all of the matters said to contribute to a breach of the implied term or trust and confidence were made out:
‘89. We have set out above our findings on all the allegations under the constructive dismissal heading and that the claimant has established that all of these alleged acts occurred as a matter of fact.
We find that handling of the incident on 7 February 2023 with MH including blaming the claimant and threatening her with disciplinary action if she did not attend mediation with MH, lack of support relating to the shoplifting incident on 25 January 2023 all individually amount to a fundamental breach of the duty of trust and confidence. We find that the respondent erroneously and without reason failed to adequately investigate her serious complaints about her fears for her safety or address any concerns that she raised, even when raised in a formal manner through her written complaints. The claimant raised complaints on more than one occasion, a number of managers were involved, they did not adequately consider her claims, they did not adequately consider them or assess what some individuals told them, they made unfounded assumptions and she was inappropriately blamed. The respondent went further than a failure to properly investigate, it blamed the claimant without good reason and without even having being able to identify (what she realistically rather than abstractly and therefore what was not actually available to her) should have done differently in the situations which she faced.
Further, we have found that the claimant suffered direct sex discrimination and detriments on the grounds of having blown the whistle. These are fundamental breaches of the duty of trust and confidence.
Taking all of the allegations together, we find that the duty of trust and confidence was broken. We recognise that the deletion of the body worn camera footage was not the most serious breach. However, given the seriousness of the breaches we have mentioned above, and all the breaches combined we find that this was a qualifying final straw. We find that the claimant was at the point of despairing that her real and genuine concerns would be dealt with and that she was exposed to a potentially threatening and dangerous situation at work from which the respondent would not provide any protection to her. This final straw demonstrated that it would not properly investigate her serious concerns instead it would blame her without good reason. It is symptomatic and a continuing chain of the respondent not giving her complaints due care and attention and the support and care to her with which she should have been provided.
We find that the respondent fundamentally breached the duty of trust and confidence, that deleting the body worn footage on 13 March 2023 was the last straw.’
The Tribunal found that the claimant resigned in response to the fundamental breach.
The remedy hearing and findings
Judge Pilgerstorfer KC made an order, sealed on 13 August 2025, for a transcript of the remedy hearing on 7 June 2024 to be prepared at the claimant’s expense. The purpose of the transcript was to establish whether points made on appeal were argued at the original hearing and whether the Tribunal had erred in its interpretation of the evidence available to it as to the claimant’s ill health.
It is apparent from the transcript that, on the morning of 7 June 2024, the EJ gave an oral liability judgment with reasons. The EJ then discussed with the parties how remedy would be dealt with. After that discussion, there was a short adjournment for respondent’s counsel to adjust her submissions. The claimant was cross examined about her receipt of Universal Credit, her ill health, and what she had done by way of mitigation. She was taken to some GP records which were in the bundle before the Tribunal, but which were not before me on this appeal. She was also questioned about the causes of her injured feelings. The morning concluded with the respondent’s submissions; the EJ then asked the claimant if she had anything to say. The claimant made some brief submissions. The Tribunal took an extended lunch break and gave a decision on remedy in the afternoon.
The following sections of the transcript are relevant when considering the challenge which the claimant makes to the calculation of interest on the injury to feelings award. The Tribunal selected a midpoint between the first act of sex discrimination and the final one as the date from which interest should run. The claimant challenges that approach. The discussion of interest was recorded as follows (Ms Zielinska being the respondent’s counsel):
'MS ZIELINSKA: …With regards then to the final matters on the schedule of loss we’re dealing with interest and tax liability. On interest, the respondent would accept that this ought to be awarded on any award for injury to feelings from the date of the discriminatory act at 8 per cent.
Now, whilst since we’re dealing with two different dates, perhaps we could take the
midpoint of those two for the sake of interest. I certainly wouldn’t have any objection to that.
I note for the tribunal’s benefit --
JUDGE BARTLETT: What would that date be?
MS ZIELINSKA: I can -- perhaps if I calculate the same, I can indicate that -- give an indication to the tribunal after lunch.
JUDGE BARTLETT: Yes.
….
JUDGE BARTLETT: There’s interest to be applied to the injury to feelings. I wasn’t quite sure where the midpoint was. Ms Zielinska, you indicated you might have a date for that.
MS ZIELINSKA: Thank you, judge. I’ve taken the midpoint of between 23 September 2021 and 7 February 2023, which is the 1 June 2022. 1 June 2022. So that’s 251 days either side of that.
JUDGE BARTLETT: Okay.
MS ZIELINSKA: And I’d assume it would be 8 per cent from that point, which I can
calculate shortly.
JUDGE BARTLETT: It is 8 per cent from that point, yeah.
MS ZIELINSKA: So I’ll just … that would include the aggravated damages as well. I will add those together. So the interest figure that I’m getting for 8 per cent from 1 June 2022 to today’s day would be £3,718.14.
JUDGE BARTLETT: That sounds roughly right numerically to me. Ms Oziel, do you have any disagreement with that?
MS OZIEL: No, because I have no position on that.'
The claimant also challenges the Tribunal’s finding that she had a pre-existing mental health condition, insofar as that may have been factored into the Tribunal’s assessment of injury to feelings. The transcript records that the claimant was cross examined about her GP records. Counsel appears to have been exploring with her whether there was evidence that she was unfit for work after she left the respondent’s employment. That was relevant to mitigation of loss. This passage of the cross examination is relevant:
‘Q. Okay. We can see in this document on page 456 it says “significant past” and we’ve got there “depression and mixed anxiety and depressive disorder”. Now, the numbers on the left-hand side are those indicative of when those problems arose for you?
A. I don’t know. I don’t know what that mean, because according to the GP I still have depression and anxiety, so I don’t know what it’s been put it on “significant past”, because the date it’s been diagnosed or because it’s been ongoing, I don’t know. As I say, I don’t know. What I’m trying to say it will be wrong to say that it’s not ongoing because it’s appeared on the list as “past” considering that I do have depression and anxiety according to the GP as ongoing issue. What I’m trying to say.
Q. We know we’ve got the -- so actually, no, perhaps I’ll just for the tribunal’s benefit go through this first. So if you could just turn over the page, we can see here some records of what you’ve prescribed in respect of your mental-health condition. If you turn over the page a couple of times again, page 459, we’ve got a list there of current significant, minor and then past significant and minor problems. So we can see that they’ve listed “mixed anxiety and depressive disorder, depression and anxiety disorder” under past problems. So in your -- given that that’s not necessarily consistent with your amended schedule of loss, are you saying the GP records are incorrect because those conditions are ongoing.
A. No, I’m not. I think it’s been put in correct. But if you look -- if you please look in the bottom in 460, you will see “depression” just on 11 January 2023. So what I believe it seems to me that every time that there is issue going on but there is not like a review, there is no update on it, so it stays in the past until it’s on this year. So you can see “depression” on 11 January 2023, which was happening. Then you can see the sick notes, you can see everything, but again those records have been provided quite long ago. So I believe if now, considering that I was asking them sick notes, considering that I’ve been assessed in this year, I don’t know but probably and very likely that if I would open the records, it will show “present”. But again I don’t know. I will have to check that. I don’t know why it’s been put in this way. I don’t know. It doesn’t make sense to me.
Q. All right. I’ll just make a quick note. And just --
Sorry. And you can see also “past minor problem” is “anxiety disorder”. Just 15 March 2023, so you can see it’s all ongoing but it’s appearing this way. I don’t know why.’
There is then this further passage:
‘A. No. I will say that the most impact was quite in the end. That the fact -- the reason why I put on the schedule of loss was because it was rooted in there. What I mean by that, I’ve been diagnosed with depression and anxiety in the end of 2021, beginning of 2022, which was directly related from work. Then other episode of depression was also related to work. That’s what it was important for me. But in terms of really mental injury, really going through those severe period of times were linked to the end of my employment, rather than beginning.’
The Tribunal found that the claimant should be awarded loss of earnings for 74 weeks, which represented her loss to the date of hearing and for a further three months.
In this section, the Tribunal recorded:
‘96.1.2. There was some medical evidence provided to us which showed that the claimant had depression and anxiety which pre-dated the events in question. However, we also accepted the claimant’s evidence that the events that form part of this claim seriously and detrimentally affected her mental health. We accepted her evidence that she was significantly affected by the shoplifting event and the events of which she complained about which included the threats to her person, the failure of the respondent to address this and her fears and the respondent repeatedly blaming the claimant for the difficulties she experienced. The Tribunal asked the claimant if she was applying for jobs and what jobs they were. She gave some examples and stated that she was not successful at some interviews and for others she got anxiety on the way to the interview and could not attend the interview. We accepted this evidence as we accepted her evidence about her poor mental health.’
[Emphasis added]
The Tribunal found that a 20% uplift for failure to follow the Acas Code would have been appropriate but did not apply that uplift because the statutory cap for compensation in ‘ordinary’ unfair dismissal claims had already been reached.
The Tribunal made an injury to feeling award in the middle of the middle band of Vento, £21,000. It said:
‘We consider that this was not one of[f] conduct. It continued over a period of time and involved multiple actors.
The conduct was serious and ultimately led to dismissal,
The impact on the claimant was significant, she had suffered from depression and anxiety previously but we accept her evidence that the events in question were detrimental to her mental health
We do not consider that this was the most serious sort of conduct and so the award was not in the higher band;
Taking all the facts as we have found them into account we consider that the middle of the middle band is the correct placing of the award.’
The Tribunal awarded £2000 by way of aggravated damages. There is no challenge to that award.
There was no Acas uplift applied to the injury to feelings or aggravated damages awards. The remedy judgment is silent as to the reason for that.
On the issue of interest, the Tribunal awarded interest on the injury to feelings and aggravated damages awards:
‘99. In respect of interest we applied the rate of 8% from the midpoint of the first and last act which has been taken by agreement as 1 June 2022.’
No part of the award was grossed up for tax. Ms Zielinska, the transcript reveals, had submitted that the first £13,000 (no doubt a mistranscription for £30,000) would be tax free but accepted that anything over that sum would require to be grossed up for tax and National Insurance. In the transcript, the EJ explains that there has been no grossing up of the compensatory award because the statutory cap would reduce the sum back to the sum which was awarded. The statutory cap did not of course apply to the injury to feelings and aggravated damages awards.
The legal framework
The Tribunal’s duty to determine claims
The Court of Appeal comprehensively reviewed the authorities on what claims an employment tribunal is under a duty to determine in Moustache v Chelsea and Westminster Hospital NHS Foundation Trust [2025] EWCA Civ 185. Warby LJ said this:
'33. First, proceedings in the ET are adversarial. The range of claims that may be brought and the range of substantive or procedural answers that may be raised to those claims are defined by law, principally by statute. In any given case the primary onus lies on the parties to identify, within those ranges, which claims they wish to bring and which answers they wish to advance.
Secondly, the issues raised by the parties are those which emerge clearly from an objective analysis of their statements of case. Identification of the issues does not involve reference to other documents which do not have the status of pleadings and come later. Nor should the process be a complex or difficult one. As Eady, P said in X v Y [2024] EAT 63 [49] “That pleadings matter, including in Employment Tribunals, is not a novel or controversial point”. The EJ should not be expected to analyse a party’s case by reference to documents which come after the pleadings and do not have the same status, such as a witness statement, or by reference to submissions.
…
Of course, the contents of a statement of case must be analysed in their proper context but this does not require the ET to engage in an elaborate or complex interpretative exercise. I would adopt the words of Elisabeth Laing J (as she then was) in Adebowale v ISBAN UK Ltd UKEAT/0068/15 at [16]:
‘... the construction of an ET1 is influenced by two factors: the readers for whom the ET1 is produced, and whether the drafter is legally qualified or not. The ET1, whether it is drafted by a legal representative, or by a lay person, must be readily understood, at its first reading, by the other party to the proceedings (who may or may not be legally represented) and by the EJ. The EJ is, of course, an expert but ... should not be burdened by, or expected by the parties to engage in, a disproportionately complex exercise of interpretation ...’
Thirdly, where a party seeks the ET’s ruling on an issue that emerges from an objective analysis of the statements of case (and falls within its jurisdiction) the ET has a duty to address that issue. This is the core function of the tribunal. That does not mean that the ET has to resolve every issue that is raised in a case. Sometimes a party will not press all the claims that have been pleaded; the ET is not obliged to address those which are raised but later abandoned: see Mensah v East Hertfordshire NHS Trust [1998] IRLR 531. And the ET needs only decide enough to reach a conclusion on the claims that have been pressed. Subject to these points, however, I would accept the broad submission of Ms Monaghan KC, that the ET does not have a discretion not to consider and determine a claim that has been brought before it.
Fourthly, however, the ET’s role is arbitral not inquisitorial or investigative. It must perform its functions impartially, fairly and justly, in accordance with the overriding objective, the law, and the evidence in the case. It may consider it appropriate to explore the scope of a party’s case by way of clarification. That may, in particular, be considered appropriate in the case of an unrepresented party. Whether to do so is however a matter of judgment and discretion which will rarely qualify as an error of law such that the EAT can interfere. The ET has no general duty to take pro-active steps to prompt some expansion or modification of the case advanced by a party where that might be to their advantage. These propositions emerge clearly from a series of decisions of this court and the EAT.
We have been referred to the decisions of this court in Mensah (above) at [28] and [36] and Muschett v HM Prison Service [2010] EWCA Civ 25, [2010] IRLR 451 [31]. I do not consider it necessary to review those two cases in further detail. That was done in Drysdale v Department of Transport [2014] EWCA Civ 1083, [2014] IRLR 892 where the court subjected the relevant authorities to a detailed analysis from which Barling J (with whom Arden and Christopher Clarke LJJ agreed) derived the following general principles:
It is a long-established and obviously desirable practice of courts generally, and employment tribunals in particular, that they will provide such assistance to litigants as may be appropriate in the formulation and presentation of their case.
What level of assistance or intervention is “appropriate” depends upon the circumstances of each particular case.
Such circumstances are too numerous to list exhaustively, but are likely to include: whether the litigant is representing himself or is represented; if represented, whether the representative is legally qualified or not; and in any case, the apparent level of competence and understanding of the litigant and/or his representative.
The appropriate level of assistance or intervention is constrained by the overriding requirement that the tribunal must at all times be, and be seen to be, impartial as between the parties, and that injustice to either side must be avoided.
The determination of the appropriate level of assistance or intervention is properly a matter for the judgment of the tribunal hearing the case, and the creation of rigid obligations or rules of law in this regard is to be avoided, as much will depend on the tribunal’s assessment and “feel” for what is fair in all the circumstances of the specific case.
There is, therefore, a wide margin of appreciation available to a tribunal in assessing such matters, and an appeal court will not normally interfere with the tribunal’s exercise of its judgment in the absence of an act or omission on the part of the tribunal which no reasonable tribunal, properly directing itself on the basis of the overriding objective, would have done/omitted to do, and which amounts to unfair treatment of a litigant.
The following analysis seems to me correct in principle and consistent with the case law. The starting point is to consider what claims emerge from an objective analysis of the statements of case. A failure by the tribunal to identify and address those claims is liable to amount to a breach of its core duty and hence an error of law. A failure to identify and determine a claim that does not emerge from such an analysis can amount to an error of law but only in rare or exceptional circumstances of the kind outlined in Drysdale. It is in this overall context that the role of an agreed list of issues falls for
consideration.
A list of issues is not a pleading but a case management tool. The main purpose of such a document is to summarise the existing pleadings not to amend them. On the other hand, as Mensah shows, a party may conduct itself in such a way as to lose the right to have the ET decide a pleaded issue, thereby reducing the scope of the tribunal’s corresponding duty. An agreed list of issues is one way in which that could in principle be done. Such a list is, after all, an express agreement that the tribunal should conduct the proceedings in a particular way, and an invitation to the tribunal to do so. A tribunal will usually be entitled to confine its attention to the issues on the list. By way of exception, however, it may be necessary in the interests of justice to depart from even an agreed list. There are at least two distinct categories of situation in which that may be so. The first is where a pleaded claim has been omitted from the list in circumstances that do not amount to abandonment of the claim. The second is where the claim has not been pleaded but the fundamental duty of fairness makes it necessary (that is to say, essential) that it should be raised and considered.’
Later in the judgment, Warby LJ referred to another authority which was highly relevant to the appeal before me, the decision of HHJ Auerbach in McLeary v One Housing Group Ltd UKEAT/0124/18. In McLeary, the claimant brought claims of unfair constructive dismissal and various types of disability discrimination. She did not have legal representation. At a preliminary hearing, her discrimination claims were dismissed as being out of time. Her unfair dismissal claim had been presented in time. The claimant appealed on the basis that the tribunal should have identified that there was also a complaint of discriminatory constructive dismissal, which was also presented in time. The claimant in that case had not expressly identified that she was bringing a claim under section 39 of the Equality Act 2010 nor said in terms that she was complaining that her dismissal was discriminatory. In the list of matters said to give rise to the constructive dismissal, the claimant set out allegations about failures to make reasonable adjustments and other failures to support the claimant in relation to her disability. At a case management hearing a list of issues was drafted which identified that the conduct the claimant relied on included failure to make reasonable adjustments and harassment.
HHJ Auerbach said that it was:
‘clear, and accepted by Mr Bryan, that she was claiming that a number of episodes or incidents of treatment that she said amounted to discriminatory treatment, or were otherwise contrary to the Equality Act contributed, along with other episodes and incidents, to what she said was the overall breach of the implied duty of trust and confidence, which in turn founded her assertion that she had been constructively dismissed.’
HHJ Auerbach considered how the issues should have been dealt with at the case management stage:
'88. I have also considered whether it might be said that it would not be appropriate for the Tribunal, as it were, to invite a claimant to add a wholly new complaint. Indeed, it would not. However, what was necessary here, starting with the Case Management Hearing, was simply to clarify the substance of what the Claimant was saying and the claims that she was seeking to bring. A margin of appreciation should indeed be allowed to the Judge below, as to how such matters are managed; but when, as in this case in my judgement, it shouts out from the contents of the Particulars of Claim that it is being alleged that there have been a number of acts of disability discrimination that have, along with other acts, contributed to an undermining of trust and confidence that has driven an employee to resign. and the employee is effectively a litigant in person and has no professional representation, this is a matter that should, at the very least, be raised at the Case Management Preliminary Hearing so that clarification can be sought.
…
Drawing all the threads together, I stress that every case will turn on its particular
circumstances, the contents of the documents, the attributes and capabilities of the litigant, and
the Judge’s appreciation of how best to manage things, in order to make due allowance for a
litigant in person, while not intervening to take their side. Generally, it must be left to the
appreciation of the Employment Judge, whether, or how, a point of this sort needs to be
proactively raised or addressed. The EAT should be slow to second guess the Judge’s approach,
and a wide margin of appreciation should be allowed. The Drysdale guidance is the touchstone.
However, the starting point is a fair reading of the pleadings. It seems to me that in this
case, on a fair reading, the Claimant’s original Particulars of Claim and/or her original Particulars
of Claim and her subsequent March pleading, should have been read as sufficient to include a
claim of constructive dismissal contrary to section 39; or, at the very least, their content was such
that the matter should have been proactively raised by the Judge at the Case Management
Preliminary Hearing and clarified, given how the point, it seems to me, jumped out from the claim
form and Particulars of Claim; and/or given that it was not in this case, raised at the case
management hearing, it should have been raised prior to or at the Preliminary Hearing on time.’
In Moustache, Warby LJ said of McLeary:
‘ In my view the ratio decidendi of the case is that on an objective reading of the statements of case in their proper context the employee was claiming that her constructive dismissal flowed from acts of discrimination. The judge did say, further and alternatively, that the issue “should at least have been raised and clarified by the tribunal at the initial case management hearing” In reaching that conclusion the judge referred to Drysdale and made clear that he regarded his conclusions as consistent with the principles there identified. I therefore read this alternative ground of decision as a finding that if (contrary to the judge’s primary conclusion) the discrimination claim was not clearly pleaded then, on the facts of the case, the claim was so obvious that it was perverse of the tribunal not to identify it’.
As to the status of the list of issues, Warby LJ referred to Mervyn v BW Controls Ltd [2020] EWCA Civ 393, [2020] ICR 1364 and summarised the guidance of Bean LJ that at a full merits hearing, the tribunal should consider:
‘45....whether any list of issues previously drawn up “properly reflects the significant issues in dispute”; if it is clear that it does not or that it may not do so the tribunal should consider whether an amendment to the list of issues is “necessary in the interests of justice” within the meaning of Rule 29; that will depend on a number of factors, including the stage at which the issue arises, whether the list was agreed between legal representatives, and whether an amendment would delay or disrupt the hearing; on the facts of Mervyn it was necessary in the interests of justice for the list to be amended so that the tribunal could consider constructive unfair dismissal.’
He also discussed the judgment of Eady J in Z v Y[2024] EAT 63:
‘47...The facts differed from those of the cases I have been considering in that this employee’s ET1 expressly pleaded a claim of discriminatory constructive dismissal. A list of issues was drawn up and agreed thereafter. The ET concluded that discriminatory constructive dismissal was not an issue before it because it did not feature in the agreed list. In the EAT the employee argued that this conclusion was “perverse” because (among other things) a claim for discriminatory constructive dismissal was sufficiently pleaded and/or the ET was not required to “stick slavishly to the list of issues agreed where to do so would impair the discharge of its core duty ...” Eady P allowed the appeal. The essentials of her reasoning appear from the summary at the head of the judgment and paragraphs [54]-[55].
‘Summary
The ET erred in failing to determine the claim of discriminatory constructive dismissal which was part of the pleaded case before it; the list of issues had not replaced the pleaded claim and the ET had been wrong to slavishly stick
to that list (Parekh … applied)
…
… it is helpful to start with what is not in dispute. First, as part of her pleaded case, the claimant had made clear that her claims of disability discrimination under the EqA included a complaint of discriminatory constructive dismissal …Fourth … at no stage was she asked whether she had withdrawn that claim, which had been made plain (one might say, per Mervyn and McLeary ‘shouted out’) from the case she had originally pleaded.
55 … As the Court of Appeal made plain in Parekh an ET should not stick slavishly to the agreed list of issues where to do so would impair its core duty to hear and determine the case before it. In the present proceedings that case had included a claim of discriminatory constructive dismissal, which had never been withdrawn … Whether the ET’s failure to recognise that this was an issue in the case is characterised as perverse or as a straightforward error of law in failing to address a claim that it was required to determine, I am satisfied that it was wrong in law for the ET to decline to determine the claim of constructive discriminatory dismissal that was before it.’
Remedy issues
Compensation for 'ordinary' unfair dismissal is subject to a cap under section 124 Employment Rights Act 1996:
‘(1) The amount of—
any compensation awarded to a person under section 117(1) and (2), or
a compensatory award to a person calculated in accordance with section 123, shall not exceed the amount specified in subsection (1ZA).
The amount specified in this subsection is the lower of—
[a sum which is raised yearly], and
52 multiplied by a week’s pay of the person concerned.’
There is however no cap on compensation for discrimination and there is no cap on compensation for a number of types of automatically unfair dismissal, including dismissal for making public interest disclosures pursuant to section 103A ERA 1996: section 124(1A) ERA 1996.
Awards for injury to feelings where there are multiple types of discrimination
In Al Jumard v Clywd Leisure Ltd [2008] IRLR 345, the claimant succeeded in claims of race discrimination and other claims of disability discrimination. There was some factual overlap between the claims. The tribunal made a global award for injury to feelings in respect of all the matters it found to have been discriminatory. The claimant appealed on the basis that there should have been separate awards for each act of discrimination. Elias J held at paragraphs 48 - 51:
‘48. However, we do accept that the argument advanced by Mr Roberts, who represented the claimant, that in this case the tribunal ought to have considered the two elements of race and disability discrimination separately. We recognise that where more than one form of discrimination arises out of the same facts, it can be artificial and unreal to ask to what extent each discrete head of discrimination has contributed to the injured feelings, and there will be no error of law where the tribunal fails to do that. We respectfully agree with the decision of the EAT (Morison P presiding) in Khanum v IBC Vehicles Ltd [1999] UKEAT/685/98 paragraph 17 to like effect.
Of course, where discriminatory heads overlap, it is not simply a case of treating both forms of discrimination wholly independently and then adding the sum for each; the degree of injury to feelings is not directly related to the number of grounds on which discrimination has occurred. It may be, for example, that a tribunal takes the view that the injury to feelings in, say, a case of race and disability discrimination is not materially different from the injury that would have been experienced had itbeen race alone.
However, where, as in this case, certain acts of discrimination fall only into one category or another, then the injury to feelings should be considered separately with respect to those acts. Each is a separate wrong for which damages should be provided. Apart from that, it will help focus the tribunal’s mind on the compensatory nature of the award. We would suggest for example, that it would not at all follow that the level of awards should be the same for different forms of discrimination. The offence, humiliation or upset resulting from a deliberate act of race discrimination may quite understandably cause greater injury to feelings than, say, a thoughtless failure to make an adjustment under the Disability Discrimination Act.
Having said that, the courts have emphasised on a number of occasions, not least in Vento itself (paragraph 68), that at the end of the exercise the tribunal must stand back and have regard to the overall magnitude of the global sum to ensure that it is proportionate, and that there is no double counting in the calculation.’
Acas uplift
Section 207A of the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992 (TULRCA) provides for adjustments of compensation of up to 25% in circumstances where there has been a failure to follow the Acas Code of Practice on Disciplinary and Grievance Procedures:
‘207A Effect of failure to comply with Code: adjustment of awards
(…)
If, in the case of proceedings to which this section applies, it appears to the employment tribunal that—
the claim to which the proceedings relate concerns a matter to which a relevant Code of Practice applies,
the employer has failed to comply with that Code in relation to that matter, and
that failure was unreasonable, the employment tribunal may, if it considers it just and equitable in all the circumstances to do so, increase any award it makes to the employee by no more than 25%.’
Sir Benjamin Slade and another v Biggs and others [2022] IRLR 216 was an appeal in which the respondent challenged an Acas uplift of 25% on the basis that there was double counting with elements of the injury to feelings and aggravated damages awards. Griffiths J in the EAT at para 77 said this:
'...tribunals might choose to apply a four-stage test, in order to navigate the various
points which I have been considering in this appeal:
Is the case such as to make it just and equitable to award any ACAS uplift?
If so, what does the ET consider a just and equitable percentage, not exceeding although possibly equalling, 25%?
Any uplift must reflect ‘all the circumstances’, including the seriousness and/or motivation for the breach, which the ET will be able to assess against the usual range of cases using its expertise and experience as a specialist tribunal. It is not necessary to apply, in addition to the question of seriousness, a test of exceptionality.
Does the uplift overlap, or potentially overlap, with other general awards, such as injury to feelings; and, if so, what in the ET’s judgment is the appropriate adjustment, if any, to the percentage of those awards in order to avoid double-counting?
This question must and no doubt will be answered using the ET’s common sense and good judgment having regard to the final outcome. It cannot, in the nature of things, be a mathematical exercise. The EAT must be reluctant to second guess the ET’s decision either to adjust or not adjust the percentage in this respect, or the amount of any adjustment, because it is quintessentially an exercise of judgment on facts which can never be as fully apparent on appeal as they were to the fact-finding tribunal. The EAT will certainly not substitute its own view for the judgment of the ET in the absence of an obvious error.'
Interest on discrimination awards
A tribunal is obliged to consider making an award of interest pursuant to the Employment Tribunals (Interest on Awards in Discrimination Cases) Regulations 1996/2803. The period over which interest is to be awarded is governed by regulation 6:
‘6.—
Subject to the following paragraphs of this regulation—
in the case of any sum for injury to feelings, interest shall be for the period beginning on the date of the contravention or act of discrimination complained of and ending on the day of calculation;
in the case of all other sums of damages or compensation (other than any sum referred to in regulation 5) and all arrears of remuneration, interest shall be for the period beginning on the mid-point date and ending on the day of calculation.
Where any payment has been made before the day of calculation to the complainant by or on behalf of the respondent in respect of the subject matter of the award, interest in respect of that part of the award covered by the payment shall be calculated as if the references in paragraph (1), and in the definition of “mid-point date” in regulation 4, to the day of calculation were to the date on which the payment was made.
Where the tribunal considers that in the circumstances, whether relating to the case as a whole or to a particular sum in an award, serious injustice would be caused if interest were to be awarded in respect of the period or periods in paragraphs (1) or (2), it may—
calculate interest, or as the case may be interest on the particular sum, for such different period, or
calculate interest for such different periods in respect of various sums in the award, as it considers appropriate in the circumstances, having regard to the provisions of these Regulations.’
There is little authority on these provisions. The tribunal in Al Jumard had awarded interest from a date later than the date of the first act of discrimination, apparently in error. The acts had occurred over a period the tribunal said was some twenty months. At paragraph 58, Elias J said:
'Interest
In relation to the question of interest, the complaint is that the tribunal failed to appreciate that the first act of discrimination arose out of the warning given in May 2002 when the alarm was set off. It is true that the tribunal appears to have forgotten that since they fix the first date as at December 2003. It is, however, right to say that the more substantial complaints started in December 2003, as the tribunal noted. We would been reluctant to refer this matter back to the tribunal had it been the only complaint, but since the other issues are being reconsidered, the tribunal should look at this point also and see if and to what extent it makes any material difference to their analysis.'
In Derby Specialist Fabrications Ltd v Burton[2001] ICR 833, the claimant had suffered racial abuse which the tribunal accepted was part of a continuing policy or practice of discrimination which ultimately resulted in what was found to be a discriminatory constructive dismissal two years after the first act of harassment. One of the grounds of appeal was as to the period of interest awarded. Keene J said:
‘38. It is contended by Mr Clayton that the tribunal has overcompensated the respondent by awarding interest on the £5,000 for the whole of the period during which injury to feelings had taken place. The £5,000 reflected acts of discrimination taking place after April 1996 and indeed injury to feelings which grew more severe in May and June 1998. Where a tribunal decides that there is a continuing discriminatory act (covering two years) the compensation it awards will reflect an assessment of the proper amount to be paid at the end of the period covered. Therefore, there is no justification for awarding interest calculated by reference to the beginning of the act. Consequently the appellant submits that the tribunal should have exercised its powers under Regulation 6(3) so as to award interest from the midpoint of the period between April 1996 and the date of the award. It is said that it was perverse of the tribunal not to have done so.
It is clear that Parliament intended that, unlike interest on other awards where the midpoint was to be taken, interest on an award for injury to feelings should normally be from the date of the discriminatory act. That must be taken to allow for the fact, of which Parliament cannot have been ignorant, that the injury to feelings is not a one-off event but something which will often persist over a period of time. So the mere fact that any award for such injury to feelings reflects injury occurring over a period of time cannot of itself justify a departure from the normal rule in Regulation 6(1)(a) . Parliament has clearly chosen to depart from the normal approach to interest awards in personal injury cases involving pain, suffering and loss of amenity. Mr Clayton acknowledged this in the course of argument.
Thus the point becomes whether the tribunal's reference to the injury becoming more severe during May and June 1998, a factor presumably reflected in the £5,000, required the tribunal in its discretion under Regulation 6(3) to depart from the normal rule because serious injustice would result from doing otherwise. Had it stood alone, this argument might have succeeded. But the tribunal also found that the injury to feelings had diminished between then and its decision in July 1999. So the tribunal was faced with a variation first up and then down in the gravity of the injury to the respondent's feelings.
In those circumstances it must have been open to the tribunal to decline to find that serious injustice would be caused by adhering to the normal approach. It seems to have given consideration to whether or not it should exercise those powers, since it expressly uses the phrase “it was appropriate to award interest”. The conclusion which it arrived at was not a perverse one and this tribunal is not justified in interfering with the award. This appeal will also be dismissed’.
Tax on injury to feelings awards and grossing up
Awards of compensation are subject to grossing up to reflect tax a claimant is liable to pay on the award in order that a claimant receives the amount after tax which a tribunal has calculated as the amount appropriate to compensate for the wrongs it has found. Broadly speaking, awards for injury to feelings are subject to tax if there is a sufficient connection with a dismissal ,for reasons set out by Griffiths J in Sir Benjamin Slade v Biggs:
'87. Section 401 of ITEPA [Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003] provides, so far
as material: ‘401 Application of this Chapter (1) This Chapter applies to payments and other benefits which are received directly or indirectly in consideration or in consequence of, or otherwise in connection with (a) the termination of a person’s employment …’
The phrase ‘directly or indirectly…in consequence of, or otherwise in connection with’ could hardly be broader and more ample than it is. Such wide wording does on the face of it cover more than damages for the dismissal itself. It appears expressly to cover awards for injury to feelings and aggravated damages which are made not only ‘in consequence’ of the claimants’ dismissals, but ‘in connection with them’ also.
Section 406 of ITEPA is also relevant and provides, so far as material: ‘406 Exception for death or disability payments and benefits (1) This Chapter does not apply to a payment or other benefit […] (b) on account of injury to … an employee. (2) Although “injury” in subsection (1) includes psychiatric injury, it does not include injured feelings.'
Grounds of appeal and arguments
Ground 1
This ground was presented rather differently in the claimant’s skeleton from the way it appeared in her notice of appeal but in either guise the core of the complaint was that the Tribunal erred in law in failing to recognise and determine complaints of:
Discriminatory constructive dismissal pursuant to section 39 Equality Act 2010;
Automatically unfair constructive dismissal for making public interest disclosures pursuant to section 103A Employment Rights Act 1996.
The effect of that error was that the claimant’s compensation for financial losses was capped.
The claimant said that it ‘shouted out’ from her claim form and from the list of issues that she was making such claims. Although the respondent asserted that she did not ‘press’ her claims at the hearing, she said that ‘press’ in Moustache did not mean to argue the claims orally but simply to pursue rather than abandoning them.
Further or alternatively, per Moustache, it was necessary in the circumstances, as part of its fundamental duty of fairness, for the Tribunal to raise and consider those issues.
In her skeleton argument, the claimant spoke in more detail about what she considered to be procedural unfairness; she emphasised that she was a litigant in person who had submitted an uncapped schedule of loss. There was no counter schedule to indicate to her that the respondent would contend for capped losses. The statutory cap was not referred to in the list of issues. The Tribunal did not explain the statutory cap to her and the first she became aware of it was during the respondent’s submissions on remedy. The claimant said that there was procedural unfairness in how the remedy hearing progressed in that she did not have an opportunity to consider and make submissions on the point.
Respondent’s submissions
The respondent also relied very significantly on Moustache in support of its contention that the onus was on the parties to identify the claims they wished to bring. Even where a claim emerged from an objective analysis of the pleadings, the tribunal was only obliged to decide the claims which had been pressed and had no general duty to take proactive steps to prompt an expansion or modification of the case advanced by a party.
The respondent said that the section 103A ERA 1996 and section 39 Equality Act 2010 claims did not emerge from an objective reading of the particulars of claim, as to the drafting of which she had received some legal assistance. Here the Tribunal would have known that the claimant had had representation at the case management hearing where the list of issues was agreed so would not have had to treat her as a litigant in person for those purposes. Although the list of issues contained reference to the claimant’s resignation occurring in response to ‘being discriminated against’, the list of issues was not a pleading and the Tribunal was not required to address an issue if it was not pressed by the claimant. The Tribunal could not be said to have been perverse in not pursuing these possible claims with the claimant in the circumstances.
It was alternatively argued that the Tribunal had not found that the claimant resigned in response to discrimination per se and that the Tribunal did not find that the discrimination was an effective cause of the claimant’s dismissal.

The claimant said that it was an error of law for the Tribunal to make a single award for injury to feelings in respect of claims based on different factual allegations and different statutory wrongs. She relied on Al Jumard.
Respondent’s submissions
The decision was in accordance with Al Jumard since all of the forms of discrimination arose from the same facts. The behaviour which constituted sex discrimination was part of the broader context of the claimant’s complaints which the Tribunal found the respondent failed to address properly. Ground 2.1.2
The claimant said that, having found that an Acas uplift was appropriate, the Tribunal erred in not making an uplift to the award for injury to feelings. She in fact received no uplift to the compensatory award due to the application of the statutory cap so there could have been no double counting.

The respondent argued:
The Tribunal is entitled to consider whether an uplift will overlap with other awards to avoid double counting: Sir Benjamin Slade vBiggs;

The claimant said that there was no evidence to support the Tribunal’s finding that the claimant had previously suffered from mental ill health. Discussion and conclusions
Ground 1
The facts here were very close to those in McLeary. In her claim form, the claimant had listed as breaches of the implied term or matters which contributed to breach of the implied term both the matters she relied on elsewhere in the claim form as sex discrimination and also 'clear detriments being suffered as I reported breach of legal obligation in protecting myself, staff and customers from harm.' In circumstances where some of the breaches/components of the breach are said to be discrimination and/or whistleblowing, it is difficult to see how a claim of discriminatory/ whistleblowing constructive dismissal could be said not to shout out of the claim form. An employment judge is a specialist in this area of law and the identification of these claims would not involve a disproportionately complex exercise of interpretation. In the language of the authorities, these claims were present on an objective reading of the claim form, and hence determining those claims fell within the Tribunal's core duty. In the alternative, in my judgement, they should have been identified by the Tribunal as part of its duty of fairness.
Those issues did not make their way into the list of issues agreed at the case management preliminary hearing, at which the claimant was represented by a solicitor. They are however present in that list of issues in much the same way they are present in the claim form. The matters set out under the constructive dismissal head included 'Being discriminated against (see) below' and a series of matters which were also relied on as whistleblowing detriment, including the 'last straw'. There is also a number of incidents which are neither. The matters relied on which took place in early 2023 were almost all said to be sex discrimination or whistleblowing detriment. As the claimant pointed out, these were the last matters which occurred and which led directly to her resignation.
It does not seem to me in those circumstances that the list of issues as drafted could be said to be an unequivocal abandonment of the discriminatory or whistleblowing dismissal claims or anything like it. Reading the passage from Moustache in which the expression 'pressed' is used and noting the reference to Mensah, I agree with the claimant that what it is intended to mean is certainly something closer to 'not abandoned' than 'pressed in submissions'.
It might be said that a tribunal at a full merits hearing should be entitled to rely on a list of issues agreed by legal representatives as setting the parameters of the claims to be determined, and in many cases that will be so. As per para 40 of Moustache, however, it may be necessary in the interests of justice to depart from an agreed list. In this case there were two claims hiding in plain sight, both in the claim form and in the list of issues itself. The claimant had been at best sporadically represented and the Tribunal expressly recognised that the list of issues was imperfect and that it should not slavishly follow it.
In those circumstances, in my judgement, it was part of the Tribunal's duty of fairness to explore whether claims of discriminatory and/or whistleblowing dismissal were pursued. In other words, it should not have stuck slavishly to the list of issues at the expense of claims which were present in the claim form and had not been abandoned, per Z v Y. The identification of those claims at the outset of the full merits hearing would not have caused any material disruption to the hearing; the evidence to be called would be the same. The additional legal labels might have led to some additional cross examination of the claimant about her reasons for resigning. The Tribunal comes very close to recognising the implications of its own findings at paragraph 91 of the reasons, where it says in terms that the sex discrimination and whistleblowing detriments were 'fundamental breaches of the duty of trust and confidence'.
It could not be said, as the respondent argued, that the Tribunal made a finding that discrimination was not an effective cause of the dismissal in circumstances where it simply did not address the issue.
I have allowed the appeal on Ground 1 on the basis that these claims should have been identified by the Tribunal at the liability stage. I have therefore not gone on to consider in detail the claimant's arguments that unfairness arose at the remedy stage because of the way in which the issue of the statutory cap was raised and unfolded. I simply observe that, unless the Tribunal had decided to reconsider its liability decision, the issue of whether or not impose the statutory cap was not open to debate at the remedy stage, as the Tribunal had not found the claimant's dismissal to be unlawful in a way which would lead to uncapped compensation.
Ground 2.1
Al Jumard is clear authority for the proposition that where the same acts are discrimination on the basis of more than one protected characteristic, one award for injury to feelings is likely to be appropriate but 'where, as in this case, certain acts of discrimination fall only into one category or another, then the injury to feelings should be considered separately with respect to those acts.' Whistleblowing injury is treated in the authorities as analogous to discrimination injury and the guidance in Al Jumard must be taken to apply to cases where there are some acts which are discriminatory and others which are whistleblowing detriment.
In this case, the claims arose in a common factual context and had causal relationships with one another. The second incident of discriminatory conduct by Mr Henderson gave rise to the disclosure and the disclosure in turn gave rise to the detriments but the acts and actors themselves were distinct and required to be analysed separately. To this extent, there was an error by the Tribunal and this ground of appeal is also allowed. It may be that analysing injury to feelings in this way results in little if any change to the overall award; that will be a matter for the Tribunal to assess.
Ground 2.1.2
The Tribunal found that an uplift for failure to follow the Acas Code was appropriate and that the percentage it would have awarded was 20%. The Tribunal concluded there was no need for it to assess the amount of the uplift in respect of the compensatory award because the claimant's loss of earnings would take her over the statutory cap before the uplift was applied. It was silent on the question of whether to apply an uplift to other parts of the award.
The assessment of the amount of uplift is very much a matter for the Tribunal which heard the evidence and the Tribunal would have to be alive to the risk of double counting. The difficulty is that there is simply no reference in the reasons to what consideration the Tribunal gave to this issue. I did not accept Mr Welch's proposition that, having made a finding that an uplift is appropriate, a tribunal need only go on to consider the application of that uplift to heads of loss in the schedule where the uplift has been expressly referred to. Once the Tribunal has found there has been an unreasonable failure to follow the Acas Code, it has a discretion as to whether to apply an uplift to the various heads of loss. A failure to consider the question in relation to a potentially relevant head of loss is a breach of the core duty. In those circumstances, the Tribunal has either erred in not considering the issue of uplift in relation to the injury to feelings award or has erred in not providing reasons for a decision not to apply the uplift. The claimant's failure in her schedule of loss to perform a calculation for uplift on the injury to feelings award cannot, particularly in the context where she was an unrepresented litigant, properly be construed as a decision not to pursue the uplift on that part of the award.
Ground 2.2
It was common ground that there was no evidence before the Tribunal that the claimant had a history of anxiety and depression predating the first act of discrimination. The Tribunal found she did have such a history. It appears from the transcript that this misapprehension may have arisen from a line of cross examination pursued by respondent's counsel which was aimed at establishing whether the mental health problems caused by the unlawful acts had terminated by a particular point. In any event, the result is that the Tribunal has made a finding that was not supported by evidence as to the claimant's mental health history and has expressly referred to that incorrect finding in the passages of the reasons where it assesses compensation for injury to feelings. The inescapable inference is that that finding was at least a factor in the assessment of the injury to feelings award. The appeal on this ground is allowed.
Ground 2.3
I have allowed the appeal against the injury to feelings award on two specific bases. I did not consider that the claimant had also reached the high threshold for a perversity appeal. The Tribunal had weighed relevant factors, both those which tended to increase and those which tended to diminish the award and has given adequate reasons for the sum it has awarded. The sum awarded was £7,000 shy of the award the claimant contended for in her schedule of loss; the Tribunal made an award in the middle of the middle Vento band and the claimant had argued for an award towards the upper end. It is impossible to assess what, if any, effect on that sum the errors identified have made to the level of the award, but even the award as unmodified did not seem to me one which no reasonable Tribunal could have concluded was appropriate. This ground did not succeed.
Ground 2.4
The issues of interest and grossing up will have to be revisited if there are changes to the compensation which the claimant receives consequent on her successful appeal on Ground 1, so to an extent the appeal as to the adequacy of the reasons is academic. If the claimant's dismissal is found to be discriminatory and/or automatically unfair pursuant to section 103A ERA 1996, that may connect her injury to feelings with the dismissal to an extent that is likely to render the injury to feelings award taxable. Either way, in circumstances where there is a dismissal or a constructive dismissal closely connected to acts of discrimination or public interest disclosure detriment, it will usually be appropriate for a tribunal to consider whether and to what extent the injury to feelings award is made in connection with the dismissal and hence taxable. Tribunals also need to be alert to the further complication that an award for psychiatric injury will be exempt from tax pursuant to section 406 ITEPA. Given the findings that this Tribunal had made, it was obliged to explain why it had not grossed up the injury to feelings award.
So far as interest is concerned, if a tribunal makes a decision that it is in the interests of justice to deviate from the calculation provided for by regulation 6(1)(a), that is a matter which requires some explanation, which could probably in most cases be brief. It may be that in some cases it will be in the interests of justice for a midpoint to be taken when assessing interest on injury to feelings; the judgment of Keene J in Derby Specialist Fabrications Ltd v Burton is support for the proposition that there may be cases in which a fluctuation in the degree of injury to feelings justifies a departure from the standard approach. As that judgment also makes clear, it was not, however, the intention of Parliament that that should be the usual or default approach in cases where there are continuing acts (or, I would add, multiple acts) of discrimination. There is a wide range of possible factual scenarios and careful thought needs to be given by a tribunal as to whether and why a different method of calculation is appropriate.
The fact that the claimant did not disagree that the midpoint fell on a particular date and led to calculation of a particular sum was not an agreement by her that calculating interest from a midpoint was appropriate. That her agreement did not expressly go any wider is apparent from the transcript.
It follows that this ground of appeal also succeeds. I bear in mind that this Tribunal was doing its best to complete the disposal of the proceedings including remedy within the time listed. That was clearly in the interests of both parties and of other litigants. Remedy issues are often finicky and technical, however, and it is easy for errors to creep in when they are dealt with at speed.
Disposal
I canvassed with the parties at the hearing whether and what further factfinding might be required if the appeal was successful on Ground 1. Clearly a decision as to whether the dismissal was automatically unfair pursuant to section 103A ERA 1996 will require further findings to be made as to whether the public interest disclosure was the principal reason for the claimant's constructive dismissal. That is a decision for the Employment Tribunal and not this Appeal Tribunal.
I considered carefully, having regard to the statement of the law in Jafri v Lincoln College [2014] EWCA Civ 449, whether, on the basis of the Tribunal's findings, it could be said that there was only one answer to the question of whether the sex discrimination was a material factor in the claimant's resignation so as to establish that her constructive dismissal fell within section 39 Equality Act 2010.
The Tribunal found at paragraph 91 of the reasons that the acts of sex discrimination were breaches of the implied term of trust and confidence. What it seems to me the Tribunal has not done, (because it was not considering a claim of discriminatory constructive dismissal) is assessed whether the discriminatory acts sufficiently influenced the overall repudiatory breach. That is, per Cavanagh J in De Lacey v Wechseln Ltd (t/a The Andrew Hill Salon) [2021] IRLR 547, very much a question of fact and degree for an employment tribunal.
The remedy issues are also all matters of assessment in respect of which it cannot be said that there is only one possible outcome. Having regard to the guidance inSinclair Roche & Temperley v Heard UKEAT/0738/03, [2004] IRLR 763, I have concluded that remission to the existing Tribunal is appropriate:
- The liability judgment is not fatally flawed but is well and thoroughly reasoned in respect of the claims the Tribunal perceived to be in front of it. There is no reason to doubt the Tribunal's professionalism or ability to deal with the claims that it did not perceive it was required to decide previously;
- Although there was a number of issues with the remedy judgment, they appear to have arisen from speed and to be the result of oversight. Again there is no reason to doubt the Tribunal's ability to deal fairly and professionally with the outstanding remedy questions;
- Even allowing for the lapse of time, it is likely to be possible for the existing Tribunal to deal with the outstanding issues in a proportionate way on the basis of its existing findings and notes of evidence.

Appeal Ref: CH-2025-000167 and Claim No: CR-2025-006711
ON APPEAL FROM THE INSOLVENCY AND COMPANIES LIST ICC
JUDGE AGNELLO KC
Royal Courts of Justice, Rolls Building,
